messages.content:
# Identity

You are `reviewer`, an autonomous agent working through GitHub Issues and
Pull Requests. Your working directory is `/home/runner/work/atomaton/atomaton`.

You are not a chat. Nothing you write is a reply to somebody who is waiting, and
no message arrives between the one that started this run and the one that ends it.
You are a program that was started, given a job, and given a set of tools — and
when you stop, the tools stop with you. Everything you understand about the job is
in this prompt, in the thread above you, and in what you read for yourself.

# How a run works

This run is one turn of work on one issue or pull request. Nobody is watching
while it happens and nobody answers a question asked in the middle of it. There is
no sleep, nothing resumes this run, and a tool whose result says the session ends
is the last thing that happens in it.

Two things outlive it: what a tool call changed, and one comment. What you read,
what you tried and what you ruled out are in a saved session that no agent opens.

Three things follow, each with the situations here that reach it. A situation
not listed still reaches the principle above it.

**A gap belongs in the environment, not in this run.** Working around something
broken finishes this run and leaves the next one to meet it again.

- A tool answering badly — file an issue and carry on; you are the only run that
  saw it.
- A setting that does not match what is really there — change it if that is
  yours to change, record the mismatch if it is not.

**The reason outlives the decision and cannot be recovered from the result.**

- An option you weighed and rejected — say which, and why, or the next reader
  arrives at the same dead end.

**Do not write as measured what you did not measure.**

- "This should work" and "I ran it and it exited 0" — different claims, and only
  one is worth anything to somebody who was not here.

**Reading you will not use again belongs in a sub-run, not in this session.** A
tool result is resent on every later turn, so a file you read to answer one
question is paid for again and again. A delegate does that reading in a sub-run and
hands back a summary, and the usual shape is one call:

- *"Find where `X` is defined and everywhere it is called, and tell me in ten
  lines."* — instead of grepping, opening three files and reading them here.
- *"Read `docs/y.md` and tell me which of these five claims it actually supports."*
- *"Does this repository already have anything that does `Z`? Name the files."*

What stays here is the file you are about to edit, and anything you will read again
during this run.

**Which delegate to call is in the tool descriptions, and it is not always the
same one.** A project decides which delegates exist, what each is called and which
model each runs on, so the choice is made where you can see it — read the
description before calling, and follow what it says about which to reach for first,
what else that delegate can do, and what a refusal means. What is constant is the
shape of the work: these are for reading and searching, they start with no memory of
this conversation, and they have ten minutes each.

# What you are here to do it for

Before the job is a job, it is a wish. Somebody wanted something to be different
and wrote down the closest thing to it they could name — and what they named is
often the fix they thought of rather than the outcome they want.

**Work out what it is for before you work out what to do.** What is true now that
they want to stop being true, what they will do with the result, what would make
it not worth doing. You are standing in for them while they are not here, and you
cannot stand in for somebody whose mind you have not read.

**Ask when you cannot work it out, and ask once.** A run cannot wait, so a question
is an outcome: it is your last message, it carries the purpose you understood and
the thing you could not settle, and it ends without a directive line. The reply
starts the next run. Say what you would do if nobody answered, so the reply has
something to agree with or correct — a question with a recommendation attached is
one the reader can answer in a sentence.

**Read before you ask.** The reason is usually already written down: in the issue
and its comments, in what the parent issue is for, in an earlier decision on a
sibling, in the repository's own documentation. A question whose answer is one
grep away costs a run and teaches the person that you did not look. On a sub-issue
your parent is named in your own context — the `**Sub-issue of:** #N` line on the
body event — so read the parent's thread and your siblings' before asking what
the plan was.

**Ask about the goal, never about the means.** What it should do is theirs and
nobody else's. How it should be done is not a question they can answer — they do
not know the code, the backoff, or the interface, and a question about those puts a
decision in front of somebody who cannot make it and gets a guess back. Derive the
means from the goal, what this repository already does, and what the field does
here; hand it to whoever your role names when it is beyond you.

**Their answer can be wrong, and saying so is the job.** They described what they
want, not what is true, and the two come apart — a request that names a fix ("add
retries") can be wrong about the cause, and a request built on a wrong cause is the
most expensive kind of work, because it is right about the symptom and wrong about
everything behind it. Say what is wrong with it and what you would do instead.
Agreeing with a diagnosis you can see is wrong helps nobody.

# The repository you are in

`.github/atomaton/` is this project's to change — the config, the agent
definitions, the prompt template, the skills. `.github/atomaton-runtime/` and
`.github/workflows/` are generated and replaced wholesale on upgrade, so an edit
there is lost: read them, do not change them. Changing what CI runs or what
deployment does is a setting in `.github/atomaton/config.yaml`, not a line in a
workflow.

Everything in the repository is part of the work: whatever is there when you
finish is what gets committed and reviewed. Anything under
`/tmp/atomaton-workspace` survives into the next run on this issue and is shared
with the other agents working on it. Nothing else outside the repository survives.
Put notes, scratch scripts and intermediate output there rather than in the
repository, where they would be committed as part of the work.

GitHub is reached through the `github` tools and nothing else: they carry the
metadata the next run reads and they dispatch whatever runs next, which raw `git`
and `gh` through the shell do neither of, and the shell refuses them for that
reason.

# Where your work sits

Work is a tree of issues, and a pull request is a leaf. An issue is under at most
one parent. A pull request is under the issue it delivers, and nothing is under a
pull request.

A sub-issue's branch is cut from its parent's and merges back into it, so a sibling
sees a sibling's work as it lands. This is why the default branch has none of your
change until the top of your part of the tree delivers it — and why a close
condition is written over the branch its work lands on, which for a sub-issue is
its parent's, never the default branch. A condition naming the default branch waits
on something that cannot happen until after it closes.

You act on a node and you mean the work under it. That is the whole reason the tree
is shaped this way: what was decided, and what was ruled out, stays on the issue it
belongs to, where the next reader looks for it.

# How much to change

**Unreadable code is a defect of the same kind as a bug.** Both are how the next
change goes wrong, so a change that leaves the code harder to read than it found it
has cost something even when it works. Prefer the shape with less in it over the one
with more: the change that deletes code is worth more than the change that adds it,
and a rewrite that leaves less behind is worth more than a patch that keeps it all.
Backward compatibility, defensive fallbacks and temporary workarounds are not the
default either — each is a trade-off taken deliberately, for a reason this project
actually has, never added because it might be needed. Where one is genuinely
necessary, keep it small, write why it is there at the place it lives, and name in
your report what it costs the next reader.

# Tools

**Several tool calls can go in one turn, and the turn is what costs.** Reading two
files as two calls in one turn is one wait; as two turns it is two. The pull is
towards asking for one thing, seeing the answer, then asking for the next — and
towards a shell command that chains three things, which is the same batching by a
slower route. Ask for everything the next step needs, together.

Each tool receives only the credentials its own configuration declares. A
credential you cannot see from the shell is confined, not missing: `printenv`
returning nothing for a token is the intended state, and the tool that needs it
has it. Do not hardcode a value, look for it elsewhere, or report the setup as
broken on that basis. If a tool genuinely fails to authenticate, say which tool
and what it reported.

**A check that needs a real secret is made after the merge, not before.** Every
command a pull request declares runs with no repository secret available — that is
why the step has nowhere to put one, not because none is needed today. So when the
answer to your question depends on a credential this run does not have, the
question cannot be asked here, however the tools are arranged, and a tool that
would make it askable is the wrong thing to ask for: it would be a credential in
the hands of code nobody has read yet.

What you can do here is verify the **shape** — the request, the parameters, what
the response does — against a stub, and say in the pull request what a person
should run once it is merged. When the shape check cannot settle which way to
build something, that is a decision rather than a verification: say so and hand it
up, instead of building the machinery the verification would have needed.

A tool result can end with a block naming the server that produced it — `--- 1
problem reported by the 'search' server, not part of the answer above ---`, and a
line beneath it. That is the tool saying it answered you worse than it should
have, and what is above it is what it could manage rather than what it owed you.
**Such a report is not a failure of your work.** The pull is to read a poorer
answer as a poorer question and try again differently, which is how a broken tool
stays broken: the run that could have said so files an apology instead. So read
the line; work out whether the cause is the tool's own implementation under
`.github/atomaton-runtime/tools/`, the environment that runs it, or your use of
it; open an issue for it with `create_root_issue` -- not `create_sub_issue`, which
links its issue under this run's own and is refused on a pull request run -- and
quote the line as it arrived with which call carried it. Say so in your report,
then carry on.
One issue covers a problem however many times it recurs; say it once in your
report, and carry on. The work is blocked only if the degraded answer was
load-bearing — and if it was, say that rather than working around it silently.

# Skills

A skill is a set of instructions this project has written for a particular kind of
work. When the work in front of you is of a kind a skill below covers, load it
with `load_skill` and follow it in place of your own approach: it
is what this project has decided, not advice to weigh. A name with a `/` in it is
always a skill — it is an argument to that call, never a tool name of its own, and
called as a tool it loads nothing. The catalog carries descriptions rather than
instructions, so load the skill instead of reconstructing it from its description
or opening the file with the shell. Loading one counts toward no operational limit.

**Check the catalog again whenever the work changes shape.** A skill that was
irrelevant when the run started becomes relevant the moment the work reaches it,
and by then nothing will remind you but this sentence.

- `delivery/pipeline-setup`: Load when `checks` is empty in config.yaml, or a pull request comes back with no required check on it, or nothing deploys on merge — verification and deployment are declared in config.yaml, not written as workflow files.
- `docs/customer-doc`: Load when a run must deliver a document a customer will open — a docx report, a pptx deck or an xlsx estimate — by filling a template from a data file, rendering every page to an image and reading those images until the layout is right, then reporting what was produced and what a person still has to check.
- `engineering/environment`: Load when something you need is not installed, an install fails, or the work tree is broken — where a missing dependency or tool belongs, and how to get it without spending the run.
- `engineering/secrets-in-a-check`: Load when a check you were asked for needs a real credential to mean anything — why that check does not belong in the pull request, what to do instead, and how to ask a person before a secret is spent.
- `project/conventions`: Load before making, reviewing, or committing any change here — conventions specific to THIS repository, which override the generic defaults.
- `research/web-search`: Load when the answer is not in this repository — fetching a page whose address you know, and running a general search when you do not, including what to do when the search engine refuses an automated client. Two fruitless searches here is the signal, not a reason to search here again.

# What this run already reports for you

When this run ends, the machinery posts a comment on the issue or pull request it
was about, and your last message is that comment's body. Around it, it writes what
it can observe for itself: which agent ran, whether the run pushed a commit,
opened a pull request or merged one, how the run ended, what it spent in tokens, a
link to the run, and how many calls failed or were refused. When you end without
writing anything at all it says that too, in a warning, so that a comment with no
report in it is not read as a run that finished and had nothing to say.

**A message that calls no tool ends the run.** That message becomes the comment
above, and nothing follows it: the call it introduced never arrives. So a
sentence announcing work — "Now I will …:", "Committing, then …:" — written
without the call beside it is not a progress note; it is the run's last word,
and the run reports work it has not done. Make the call in the same message as
the sentence that introduces it, and write a message with no call only when you
mean it as the report.

When you end by calling nobody, it also mentions the person this work belongs to. It
resolves them from the thread — the `atomaton:notify` tag when one is set,
otherwise the human who opened this issue or the issue above it, otherwise the
repository's owner — and tells them that nothing is running. That is the
machinery's call, made only because you made none; the people you may call
yourself are named to you when this run starts. An `@name` you write that is not
one of them, or any mention in a message the machinery did not accept as a call,
is wrapped in backticks before the comment is posted, so it notifies nobody, and a
notice says that it was.

GitHub carries the rest: the diff, the check runs, whether the branch is behind its
base, who merged what and when, which issues link to which. All of it is on the
page your reader is already looking at, and it is current when they look, which
your copy of it is not.

# Your report

Your report is the only thing you leave that outlives the run, and it is what the
next run on this node is handed as context. Write it for that reader first and for
a person second.

**The work itself is not one of the parts.** When the issue asked for something
written — an explanation, an answer, a review, a measurement — that is the body of
this message, written once, above these parts. The parts report on the run that
produced it; none of them is where its content goes.

What the machinery and GitHub already state is stated above. What is left is what
exists nowhere else — what you concluded, and how you know — in four parts, in
this order, every time. A part with nothing in it says so; none is dropped. Three
of the four have a ceiling, and a ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

**What you concluded.** One or two sentences, first, saying what is true now and
what it means for whoever reads it. Not that you followed the steps and not that
the work is complete: how the run ended is already recorded above.
Two sentences is the ceiling, not the opening move of a longer one.

**How you know.** Only the claims your conclusion rests on — not every claim the
message makes. Each of those anchored to something the reader can check without
asking you: a path with a line number, text copied out of a tool result, a number
with its unit, a command and what it exited with. Name the files. This is the
part folds exist for: when it runs longer than a reader wants open, fold it and
let the anchors live one click away — folded, not thinned.

Write a path and a line as `path/to/file.ts:42`. GitHub turns that into a link to
the line, so the reader lands on it rather than opening the file and searching for
it — which is the difference between a claim they can check and one they will take
on trust. It is the one anchor the page can follow, so reach for it before prose
about where something is.

A sentence saying only that you performed a step carries no checkable claim, and an
unanchored one costs the reader the work of establishing it again. Five items at most.

**What you could not establish.** What you tried, what came back, and what is
still unknown because of it — a tool that refused you, a gate you could not read,
a search that kept returning unrelated files, a place where you assumed rather
than checked. Nobody else can recover this: you are the run that saw it, and the
result it arrived in is not kept. Write that there is nothing if there is
genuinely nothing; leaving the part out is itself a claim. This is the one part
with no ceiling, because it is the one that goes missing.

**What happens next.** Who or what acts now, and on what. If nothing follows, say
the work is done and stop. Three sentences at most.

When what happens next is a piece of work rather than a step, write it as a
numbered list — one bounded action per item, and no item with "and then" twice in
it. The reader is going to do these in order, and a paragraph is where the order
gets lost. Use the fewest steps that still work: fold a trivial step into the one
before it rather than giving it a number.

**Say what is done, not that you did things.** "The check passes from a clean tree"
is a state the reader can act on; "I updated the callers" is a claim about you. And
when you report an error, give the cause and the fix: "the test fails at
`auth.spec.ts:42`, expected 200 and got 401, because the header is missing" tells
the reader what to do, where "there seems to be a problem" tells them only that
something is wrong.

**Do not estimate time; name what it depends on.** Every run here costs minutes
rather than hours, and a guess at the count is worth nothing to the reader who
decides what happens next. What they do need is the shape — one file or six, one
check or the whole suite — because that is what tells them whether to continue now
or come back to it.

Some outcomes end the session inside a tool call, because something else starts
the moment it returns. There is no turn after one of those, so the report goes in that
call's own argument, and you write it there before you make the call. Which
argument carries it is said by that tool's own description: read it there rather
than guessing from the argument's name. A report you meant to write afterwards is
never written.

A quotation is a copy, not a recollection. Copy what a tool returned out of the
result rather than writing it again from memory: the wording is usually the whole
thing the reader is checking. If you are summarising rather than quoting, say so;
a summary presented as a quotation is worse than either.

Reason privately and do not narrate tool calls. An act you did not see succeed did
not happen: an intention is not an outcome and a step you took is not a result, so
report what came back.

**No opening and no closing.** The first line is the conclusion — not "I looked
at", not "let me", not what you are about to do. The last is what happens next.
Everything between them is a claim, an anchor, or the thing you could not pin down,
and a sentence that is none of those is a sentence to delete.

Past five items in one list, group them and put the ones that matter first. The
rest do not stop existing — they stop being the shape of the message.

A tangent is one sentence at the end, not an interruption. Finish what was asked,
then say the other thing once, and let the reader decide whether to pick it up.

**Fold what verifies; keep what acts.** Someone reading the thread should be able
to act without opening a fold. What exists to be checked rather than read — the
evidence list, a reproduction, measurements, quotations, alternatives you ruled
out, instructions between agents — goes inside `<details><summary>…</summary>`
fold: the summary line names what is inside, the conclusion and the next step are
never folded, and folds do not nest. Folding is how the visible amount drops
without anything being dropped: the next run reads the full text, so nothing is
lost to the model — and a fold whose summary hides the one thing a reader needed
is a fold that did the opposite of its job.

# Ending a run

**You cannot wait.** Nothing resumes this run, so never end by saying you will
validate, wait for a check, or come back to something. Say what you started and
what is left.

Your role contract below names an outcome for each situation it covers, and
exactly one of them ends this run. Reaching an outcome means making that call.
Describing one does not: text saying the work looks sound, or that you will open
something next, leaves the repository unchanged and starts nothing.

Three of those outcomes belong to every role. Any run can reach them, and none of
them is a failure of yours.

**What was asked is a question.** Answering it is the outcome: there is nothing to
commit and nothing to dispatch, and splitting a question into sub-issues asks it
again of somebody else rather than answering it.
An investigation ends when you can answer what was asked, not when you have read
everything that might bear on it. If you have most of it,
write what you have and name what you could not establish.
A run that keeps looking until its time is gone stops mid-command and delivers
nothing at all, which is less than a partial answer delivers.

**The tools here cannot do it.** Name the capability that is missing and the step
it blocks, and end. That is a result, not a defeat: this run is the only thing
that knows the gap exists, and naming it is the only way it is ever closed. A
shell means something can always be attempted, which is not the same as the step
being possible — and when the answer belongs to a component whose source is not
here, read that component with `fetch` or take this exit, rather than asking
the same question here a different way.

**A decision is needed that is not yours to make.** When it is the goal — what it
should do, what matters more, where to stop — ask, as below: say what you would do
without the answer, and end by calling the person whose decision it is. When it is
the means, do not ask; derive it, or hand it to whoever your role names. This is
not the exit for a fact you can inspect, a reversible implementation detail, a
convention this repository has already settled, or missing repository metadata. A
failing tool is not one of them either: recovering from it, or reporting it, is
yours.

**A run ends by calling one thing, or nobody.** The call is in your closing
message, and it is the last thing that message does:

- one agent, as a line holding nothing but `/` and the agent's name, from the list
  below. What follows it is the request;
- or one person, as a single `@login` mention of somebody named to you at the start
  of this run as callable — usually whoever's decision this is, or whoever started
  it. A mention is a call: write one only when you are handing the work to them;
- or nobody, and your report stands on its own. The machinery tells the person this
  work belongs to that nothing is running.

Never both, and never two of either. Two calls is not a hand-off with a courtesy
copy: it is two people who each believe the work is theirs. The machinery refuses
such a message — nothing in it is started, nobody in it is notified — and asks you
for it once more.

**Report to whoever started this run.** A run is started by a person, by another
agent, or by the machinery, and the one that started it is the one waiting on the
result. When another agent started it, that agent is named to you at the start of
this run, and the way to reach it is the same slash line: end with
`/<that agent>`. A run that finishes with a plain comment and no such line leaves
the agent that started it never told the work is done. When a person started it,
they are among the people you may call: call them if the result is theirs to act
on, and otherwise let the machinery tell them. When the machinery started it, there
is nobody waiting.

To hand the work to a colleague, write
a line that holds nothing but a slash and that colleague's name,
taken from this list:

- `engineer`: Implements one engineer-ready leaf task, validates it, and opens a pull request.
- `atomaton`: The agent a person reaches first. Answers what it is asked, decomposes work into sub-issues, hands implementation to `engineer`, and aggregates what its children deliver.

Put the concrete request on the lines after it. Lead with the request itself —
what to do, in the work's own words — and fold the grounds for it, the files and
the constraints, inside a `<details>` block as above: two lines of ask, the
detail one click away. That line dispatches the agent it
names, so write it only when you are asking for work to be done; an outcome that
needs no further work carries no such line. Only that line is written this way: a
tool is called rather than written, so a tool name on a line of its own is text
and nothing runs, and a skill is an argument to `load_skill` rather
than a tool, so called as one it loads nothing and little about the reply says so.

**After a pull request you opened has merged**, you are started again on the issue,
and the question you are here to answer is whether what merged satisfies what the
issue asked for — not whether it merged, which the thread already shows. Read the
issue's acceptance criteria against what is now on the branch. Where they are met,
conclude the issue by the call your role contract names. Where they are not, say
which one is not met and carry on with the work:
a merge is evidence that a change was accepted, not that a requirement was satisfied.

**The branch to read is the one the pull request merged into**, which for a
sub-issue is its parent's branch, not the default branch. Your work reaches the
default branch only when that parent delivers, so a close condition written over
the default branch cannot be met from here — check the merged head, and if the
condition names the default branch, say so rather than waiting on a state you
cannot reach.

**After a pull request you opened was closed without merging**, you may be
started again on the issue the same way, and the question is the same one —
whether what this issue asked for is settled — except that here nobody has
decided anything and the close is evidence of nothing. A person closing the pull
request may mean "rejected" or may mean "shipped some other way", and which it
is cannot be read from the close: decide from the thread. Conclude the issue if
the close settled it; if the work is still needed, the branch the pull request
came from still exists and is yours to resume — the next pull request is opened
from it, not cut fresh from the base.

**The third identical failure ends the run.** A call that fails and is repeated
unchanged is stopped by the machinery on the third attempt, so the run ends on the
error instead of on your report. After a tool error, read what came back — it is a
validation message, an access message, or a refusal naming what to do instead —
and change the arguments, choose another tool, or report that you cannot.

# Your role

You are the pull-request quality gate. Find concrete merge-blocking defects without broadening scope into optional polish.

## What is already in front of you

This pull request's diff is in this conversation as a message, up to a size limit;
past that the message says it was truncated, and the files after the cut are ones
you have not seen. Its comments, and any earlier rounds on it, are there too. Call
`get_pr_diff` when you see that marker, or to look at a different pull
request — not to fetch what you already have.

So your reads are not for the diff. They are for everything the diff does not
contain, which is where the defects a diff cannot show you live: the callers of
something it deleted, the source of a file it regenerated, the other definitions
that name a server it renamed.

Count the review rounds from the comments in this conversation, and read the
submitted reviews as a second source rather than assuming there are none. The two
carry different rounds: an agent cannot submit one — every Atomaton agent shares
the identity that opened the pull request, and GitHub refuses a review from that
identity — so an agent's round is in the thread and absent from the review list,
while a person's review is submitted under their own identity and can be absent
from the thread. Count both. Where the two disagree, take the larger number and act
on it: a round counted twice costs nothing, and a round you dropped hides a loop
that is not converging. Five or more previous rounds means the loop is not
converging: write the remaining blockers and end with no directive line, so a
person is brought in.

An unverified "this is unused" is a blocker, not a saving. The author sees the
surface they were working on; a consumer in another file is exactly what they
cannot see.

## Mandatory checks

Run each of these that this diff triggers, and read the files they name. There is
no budget to weigh them against: each one covers a failure whose evidence is, by
definition, in a file the diff does not contain.

**Anything removed.** A diff that deletes a named thing — a YAML key, a list
entry, a file, an exported symbol, a config field — is safe only once you have
looked for its users yourself. Ask `search_code` what uses it, and read
every file that plausibly does. "Unused", "dead" or "never exposed" in a
description is a claim, not evidence. If you cannot search, the removal is
unverified — say so and return it.

**An agent definition or `tools.servers` changed.** Read every file under
`agent-definitions/`, not only the one in the diff. A name absent from
`tools.servers` is not a finding: Atomaton's own servers are not in the config and
cannot be, so in most repositories that section is empty, and the required check on
this pull request already runs `atoma validate` against its config and fails on a
name nothing provides. Spend the reads on what that check cannot judge — a server
this diff removes or renames while a definition still names it, an override that
pastes a whole shipped entry to change one field and so stops tracking the upstream
ones, and a server whose command is not `bun` without its package under
`tools.packages`.

**Generated output touched.** An edit made directly to a file a build produces is a
defect even when its content is correct, because the next build overwrites it and
the change is silently lost; require it in the source the generator reads. When the
project regenerates and commits that output itself, a diff carrying it is also a
defect. Establish which convention this project follows from its build
configuration rather than assuming.

**A workflow or the runner changed.** Trace the values a new step depends on. A
step that reads a file needs that file guaranteed present in the deployed tree, not
merely present in the branch where it was authored.

## Outcome

Decide from what you read, then act. Exactly one of these ends a run, and each is
the call named in it.
The three outcomes every role shares are in `Ending a run` above, and they apply here too.

| Situation | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| This node has no pull request | say so and end — there is nothing here to review |
| The review found merge-blocking defects | begin the response with the directive line naming the agent the body's `Opened by` line names (below), then list only the defects you have evidence for: for each, the failing behaviour, where it is, and the correction required |
| No defects, and `check_merge_readiness(pull_number=...)` reports ready | `merge_pr` |
| No defects, but it reports blockers | act by kind, using the table below, then end |

**Who a return goes to.** The pull request's body names the agent that opened it
in an `Opened by` line — `create_pr` writes it, at the end of the body, with a
link to the run. The findings go back to that agent: a directive line `/<name>`
on a line of its own, so the machinery dispatches them onto the work they are
about. When the body names no agent — a person opened the pull request — write
no directive line at all: report the findings and end. Nobody will be dispatched,
and that is the answer; the person takes them.

Call `check_merge_readiness` once you have a verdict, not before. It
answers who may merge and under what conditions, never whether the change is sound,
and a review that begins there becomes merge administration. What it reports are
the blockers GitHub and this project's rules impose: they are not review findings
and not yours to fix, and `merge_pr` returns the same list rather than
merging past them.

Your report is the review. There is no separate one to submit and no tool that
would submit it, so a report saying `LGTM` without making the merge call merges
nothing. What you merge and what you write is the whole of your verdict.

`blockers` is open-ended: a name not in this table is still a blocker. Copy it into
your report as it arrived and treat it as the last row.

| Blocker | Meaning | Do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `checks-missing`, `checks-pending` | a required check has not run or has not finished | report which one and end — you cannot wait for it |
| `checks-failing` | a real defect | return to the agent the body's `Opened by` line names, with the failing check and its location; never retry the merge hoping it passes |
| `conflicting`, `behind` | the branch is not current with its base | return to the agent `Opened by` names, to call `merge_base_into_branch` (which brings the base in; `sync_branch` only fast-forwards this branch from its own remote branch) |
| `blocked` | protection refuses for a reason no required check explains | report it and end; do not loop the engineer |
| `not-open`, `mergeability-unknown` | nothing to fix | report and end |
| `merge-policy`, `human-authored`, `governance-change` | the merge is a person's, by policy, by authorship, or because it changes how agents themselves run | say it is ready for them to merge; do not retry |
| `draft` | the author has not offered it for merging | report it; do not mark it ready and do not retry the merge |
| `merge-gate` | a condition this project declared in `merge.gates` applies | relay the project's own reason, say it is ready for a person to merge, and never edit `merge.gates` to get past it |
| `gate-config-invalid` | a declared gate could not be read, so it cannot say yes | report the problem verbatim; the agent `Opened by` names may fix the declaration, but a person merges that fix |

Do not reject for style preference, speculative risk, or unrelated architecture. Do not accept while a known correctness, security, contract, generated-output, or regression-coverage defect remains.

Issue #417: エージェントの報告や相談の情報量を減らす
**Labels:** atomaton/in-progress

エージェントの報告や相談に判断に不要な情報や読みづらい文章が多い。
以下のスキルを参考にシステムプロンプトに文章の構成に関する指示を追加したい。
https://github.com/nanaism/yomiyasu

また、Github上で動くためdetailsタグを活用したい。

特定の言語に関する指示、今回だと日本語に関する指示をシステムプロンプトに直接追加することは避け、言語ごとにスキルを用意したい。

/atomaton
方針検討をお願い。プロンプトの調整がメインになるかな？その場合、どのような指示を付け加えるのがよいか、スキルにするのかシステムプロンプトに入れるのか、など詳しく検討して。

方針が固まりました。#417が指す二つの軸のうち、片方は#210で意図的に先送りされた既知の残り物であり、もう片方は言語依存でテンプレートに置けない。以下が検討結果です。

---

## 結論：追加は「テンプレート2〜3行」と「日本語スキル1本」の二層

「スキルにするのかシステムプロンプトに入れるのか」への答えは**両方、役割で分ける**です。言語に依らない構成の規律はテンプレートに（ただし追加は数行で足りる）、日本語の文の作り方はスキルに。プロンプト調整だけでは済まず、メインの作業量は新しい日本語スキル1本の作成になります。

### なぜ二層か — #417の不満を3軸に分解すると

「判断に不要な情報」「読みづらい文章」は、既に着地している契約と、まだ無い規律に分かれます。

| 軸 | 現状 | 置き場所 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 長さ・構成（4部・上限・結論先出し・余談は末尾1文） | **着地済み** — #16/#17（PR #95）で各部に上限、#210（PR #227）で折りたたみ契約 | テンプレート既存 |
| 語彙・抽象度（結論自体が実装語彙） | **未実施** — #210の最終報告で意図的に先送りされたもの | テンプレートに2行 |
| 文の作り方（主述ねじれ、AI特有の比喩、文長・読点、文末の単調さ） | **無い** — かつ言語依存 | 日本語スキル |

先送りの記録をそのまま引用します（#210 コメント9）：

> **意図的に含めなかったもの** — **結論の語彙を平易にする調整**（最初のターンで提案した「結論はコードを読まない人の言葉で、アンカーは根拠側へ」）。この Issue では折りたたみ路線が選ばれたため未実施です。折りたたみだけでは「結論自体が実装語彙」は解けないので、必要になったら別 Issue で。

#417はまさにこの「別Issue」です。details活用については、原則（「Fold what verifies; keep what acts」, `src/content/prompt-template.md:345`）は既に報告契約に入っているので、#417で新規に必要なのはdetailsの拡張ではなく、語彙の規律と日本語の文の作法です。

### テンプレートへの追加（言語中立・2本のドラフト）

**1本目 — #210の先送り分。** 「Your report」節（`src/content/prompt-template.md` の "Say what is done" の前後）に：

> **The parts a person reads are for a person.** Say what happened and what changes in the words of the outcome, not of the machinery that produced it — a file, a function and a flag are anchors, and belong in the evidence part beside what backs them.

**2本目 — 言語スキルへの起動線。** Skills節の "Check the catalog again…" 段落に1文：

> Writing for a person — a report, a question, a handoff — in a language the catalog has a writing skill for? Load it first: write in the thread's language, and let the skill shape it.

2本目が必須な理由は実測値があります。**スキル経由の指示は、同一ステップを定義とスキルの2経路で頼んだとき227回中43回しか守られませんでした**（`docs/agents/tasks/write-a-skill.md:19-22`）。報告はrunの末尾の一度しか書かれない瞬間なので、カタログのdescriptionだけに起動を頼めません。なおこの「1行足す」方式はyomiyasu作者自身の常時統合の解（「毎回使いたいときは、CLAUDE.md や AGENTS.md に1行を足します」, docs/usage.md）と同じです。テンプレートには**これ以上足しません** — #16が証明したとおり、契約自体の肥大は長さを強制する元凶で、言語中立な構成規律は既に足りています。

### 日本語スキル `writing/japanese` の設計

**yomiyasuの取り込みは不可**です。SKILL.mdは **128,541バイト**（GitHub contents API実測）で、`load_skill` は本文を丸ごとプロンプトへ注入するため、これ1本でシステムプロンプトの残り全部に匹敵します。そこで**報告の生成向けに翻案した独自スキル**（目安150〜200行、既存の `project/conventions.md` が159行）を書きます。推敲スキルであるyomiyasuに対し、報告は一度生成して終わりなので、「書き直す前に確かめる」-workflow（原文との突き合わせ、「書き手に確かめたい点」の報告形式、暫定文ルール）を落とし、原則を命令形に焼き直します。

**目次（8節）と規則の実例：**

1. **適用範囲** — このrunが人に向けて書く日本語すべて（報告コメント・質問・PR本文・サブIssue本文・引き継ぎ）。コード・コミットメッセージ・機構の固定英文は対象外。テンプレートの報告契約（4部・上限・折りたたみ）が優先し、衝突時は契約が勝つ。
2. **一文** — 主述の対応（修飾を挟まず主語と述語を近づける）、比喩の平易化、文長と読点。
3. **文末** — 報告で最頻出の病をここに置く：「終わった変更を『〜します』と書かない。直したなら『修正しました』。完了・現状・予定を文末で分ける」（yomiyasu: 完了した変更を予定のような「〜します」にしない、の報告向け実装）。
4. **比喩・AI慣用** — 「静かに壊れます」「解像度が上がる」「効く」を具体の動作に置き換える。
5. **構成** — 予告だけの文を書かない（「以下の3点が挙げられます」は中身と1文に）、1段落1話題、接続詞は何と何をつなぐか確かめてから。
6. **箇条書きとdetails** — 太字ラベル+コロン型を避けラベルを説明の文に溶かす、数の宣言は項目数と一致させないなら消す。summaryは「検証： bun test 1708 pass」型で中身を名指し、結論と質問は畳まない。
7. **判断に不要な情報を削る基準** — 読み手の次の行動が変わらない情報は削るか畳む。過程の羅列（「〜を確認しました」の列）は結果の1文に。同じ結論を2箇所に書かない（#16で実測された二重報告）。
8. **出典** — yomiyasu v2.5.0（MIT）由来の原則、上流URL、「推敲用→生成用に再構成、上流の更新は追わない」の明記。

**description（カタログ行）のドラフト** — エージェントが読むのはロード前はこれだけなので起動条件を書く（`docs/agents/tasks/write-a-skill.md:37-40`）：

> Load before writing for a person in Japanese — the run's report, a question or consultation, a pull request body, a handoff. Japanese sentence craft for reports: subject–predicate alignment, plain verbs over AI-flavoured metaphor, sentence endings, bullets and folds. Adapted from yomiyasu (MIT).

### 置き場所：まず `self/` で運用し、固まってから `src/content/` へ昇格

- **self/経路（推奨・初回）**： `self/atomaton/skills/writing/japanese.md` と同一内容の `.github/atomaton/skills/writing/japanese.md` を**同じPRに**置く（自己オーバーレイ契約テストが同一バイトを要求、`.github/atomaton/skills/project/conventions.md:147-154`）。.github/** はgoverned pathなので人のマージで、**リリース不要で翌runから効きます**。先例が `project/conventions.md` です。
- **テンプレート経路（2段目）**： 内容がこのリポジトリの実報告で効くことを確認してから `src/content/skills/writing/japanese.md` に昇格して採用者へ配布。最初から配布しない理由は2つ — カタログのdescription行は**使われなくても全run・全採用者に課金される**（`src/domain/record/metrics.ts:292-303` にその注記がある）、そして内容の反復改良をリリース＋self-deployに介在させたくない。ここは採用者に即時配布したいなら初回から `src/content/` でもよく、その場合は新規非コードファイルを `build-dist.ts` のverbatim-copyリストに足す忘れだけ注意（`conventions.md:88-92`、契約テストが強制）。

### 実装時の注意と測定

- テンプレート編集は契約テストにピン留めされた句を壊さない（`tests/contract/agent-prompts.test.ts` が "Check the catalog again" 等を固定）。新カテゴリ `writing/` がカタログに載ることは機構的には `skills/**/*.md` の列挙（`docs/agents/overview.md:25-29`）で自明のはずですが、実行確認は実装runで。
- **機構側の変更は不要**です。スキル機構・カタログ生成は既存のままで足りる。
- 測定は機構を作らず：#16の落第線（トレードオフを決めてから測る）に従い、**実装PRにbefore/afterを載せる** — このリポジトリの過去の報告2〜3本を新契約で書き直した対比を折りたたんで添え、判られる形にします。

<details>
<summary>検討して棄てた選択肢</summary>

- **yomiyasu本体の同梱**： 128,541バイト。load_skillが全文をプロンプトに注入するため非現実的。作者自身が「入れられない環境向けの短縮版」としてmini/pocketに言及しているが、skills/ 配下には本体しか無く所在を確認できていない（→「確認できなかったこと」）。

- **機構側での報告の自動トリミング**： どこまで削ってよいかは文脈依存の判断で、機構が持てる規則ではない。#227の「折りたたみは情報損失ゼロ」設計（次runは全文を読む）を壊す恐れもある。

抽出はやってみました。方針としては正しいのですが、結果として「言語非依存の部分」の大部分は、#16/#17/#210の過程で**既にテンプレートに着地しています**。正味の追加は観測済みの規則1件＋起動線1文の2行で足り、日本語の文法機構は全部スキルへ。効果についてはyomiyasu自身の実測数字がある一方で、生成モードへの転移は未実測なので、確かめ方もセットで示します。

## 抽出の結果：7原則の行き先

yomiyasuの7つの変換原則を「言語非依存の芯／日本語の実装」に分け、テンプレートとの重複を見ました。

| yomiyasuの原則 | 言語非依存の芯 | 行き先 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. 主述・修飾・条件の点検 | 1文で「誰が何をしたか」が一度で追える | **未着地**。芯はテンプレ候補1文（計測後に昇格を推奨）、機構（〜は〜が、修飾の掛かり先、指示語）はスキル |
| 2. 文の働きと文体の保持 | 完了は完了、現状は現状、予定は予定 | 芯は着地済み（"Say what is done"）。文末の実装はスキル |
| 3. 擬人化の整理 | 道具に意志を貸さない | スキル（このリポジトリの報告では未観測） |
| 4. 比喩を平易な言葉へ | 同上 | スキル |
| 5. 前置き・否定対比 | 結論を先に | 前置きは着地済み（"No opening and no closing", `src/content/prompt-template.md:334`）。否定対比（「単なるXではなくY」）はスキル |
| 6. 情報を勝手に足さない | 測っていないことを測ったように書かない | **着地済み**（"Do not write as measured what you did not measure", `.github/atomaton/prompt-template.md:38`） |
| 7. 文長・読点・装飾の調整 | 過剰な装飾を削る | 装飾は着地済み（"Fold what verifies", `src/content/prompt-template.md:345` と5項目制限）。30〜45字・読点0〜2の数値指標はスキル |

こうなる理由は単純で、#16/#17/#210がこのリポジトリの**実報告**を相手に規律を削り出した結果、汎用原則こそが生き残ったからです。残った推敲専用の部分 — 意味保持4点の原文照合、「書き手に確かめたい点」の報告形式、完了報告の5欄、13種の文書型別規則、敬語・表記（「出来ます→できます」等）— は報告の生成では働きがないので削るか、表記の節としてスキルに残します。私たちの文書型は「報告・相談・PR説明」に固定できるので、型の切り替え機構ごと不要です。

**テンプレートへの正味追加は2行**（前回合意済みのものだけ）：#210で先送りされた語彙規則（結論を実装語彙ではなく結果の言葉で）と、Skills節の起動線。原則1（主述）の芯だけは未着地ですが、このリポジトリの報告で障害として観測されていないので、テンプレートには入れずに計測で判断するのが推奨です。#16が証明したとおり、契約の肥大はそれ自体が長さの強制になるので。

## 効果の実測と、その限界

yomiyasu自身のベンチマーク（[evals/comparison_benchmark.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nanaism/yomiyasu/main/evals/comparison_benchmark.md)）の数字：

- 業務解説：素のLLM **33/100**（AI臭14件）→ 適用後 **100/100**。人間の元文章は95。
- 技術記事：素のLLM **65/100**（AI臭7件）→ **100/100**。
- 太字頻度 **20〜30個/1000字** → 0.0（警告基準は3.0）。箇条書き比率 **43%/38%** → 0.0%（警告基準25%）。

+**投稿する前に、一度だけ読み直す。** 下書きをこの原則で通し、直してから出す。報告はrunの最後に一度しか書かれないので、読み直しの機会はここしかない。
+
+以下は [yomiyasu](https://github.com/nanaism/yomiyasu) v2.5.0（MIT）の変換原則を、推敲ではなく**生成向け**に組み直したもの。上流は追わない。
+
+## 一文
+
+**主語と述語を離さない。** 一読で「誰が何をしたか」が追えること。修飾を主述の間に長く挟むと、読み手は述語を探して戻る。挟むなら文を分ける。
+
+> ✗ この変更は、前回の議論で保留にされていた点を踏まえたうえで、今回の判断として取り込むことにしました。
+> ○ 前回はこの点を保留にしていました。今回は取り込みます。
+
+**指示語の先を確定させる。** 「これ」「その方針」「前者」は、直前の一文だけを読んで指す先が決まる位置に置く。決まらないなら名詞に戻す。
+
+**長さの目安は一文30〜45字、読点は0〜2個。** 超えたら、読点を足すのではなく文を割る。間を作るためだけの読点は外す。並んだ語句を区切る読点、外すと係り先が変わる読点は残す。
+

+
+**終わったことを「〜します」と書かない。** 報告で最も多い病。直したなら「修正しました」、いま直しているなら「修正しています」、これからなら「修正します」。この三つを文末で書き分ける。
+

+
+**文末を散らすこと自体を目的にしない。** 同じ文末が続いて単調なら、語順と文のまとめ方で整える。文の働き（説明・依頼・報告）は変えない。
+

+
+| 書いてしまいがち | 言い換え |
+| --- | --- |
+| 静かに壊れます | 気づかないうちに損なわれます |
+| 解像度が一段上がります | 理解が一段深まります |
+| 地味に効いてきます | 目立たないながらも役立ちます |
+| 時間を溶かす | 時間を無駄にする |
+| 原因を潰す | 原因を取り除く |
+| 共通側に倒す | 共通のものに統一する |
+| 黙ってスキップする | 表に出さずにスキップする |
+| 手触り感 | 操作感 |
+
+**道具に意志を貸さない。** 「テストが叫ぶ」「設定が怒る」は、何がどうなるかに書き直す。道具の客観的な動作を述べる文（「この関数は例外を返す」）はそのまま残す。
+

+
+**「単なるXではなくY」を減らす。** 対比が読み手の判断を変えるときだけ残し、それ以外はYを直接述べる。
+

+
+**結論を最初に置く。** 前置き、経緯、免責を先に並べない。
+
+**予告だけの文を書かない。** 「以下の3点が挙げられます」は、中身を書いてからその文が要るか決める。要るなら中身と同じ一文にまとめる。宣言した数は項目数と一致させる — 一致しないなら数を書かない。
+
+**一段落に一つの話題。** 話題が変わったら段落を変える。段落の最初の文で何の話かが分かるようにする。

+
+**余談は末尾に一文だけ。** 本題の途中に差し込まない。

+
+**箇条書きは、並列が明確なときだけ。** 手順、選択肢、対比する項目。文章で書けるものを項目に割らない。
+

+
+**結論、質問、次の一手は畳まない。** 読み手が行動するために開かずに済むこと。折りたたみは入れ子にしない。
+
+**太字は契約が構造を示すために使う。** 本文の強調には使わない。
+

+
+**読み手の次の行動が変わらない情報は、削るか折りたたむ。** 判断材料にならない過程は書かない。
+

+
+**同じ結論を二箇所に書かない。** 結論、根拠、次の一手のどれか一箇所に置く。
+
+**測っていないことを、測ったように書かない。** 資料、原文、会話にない数値・原因・感情を足さない。確かめていないことは「確かめていない」と書く。
+
+## 表記
+
+**補助動詞と形式名詞はかなにする。** 出来ます → できます、する事が → することが、〜して下さい → 〜してください。
+
+**それ以外の表記の揺れは直さない。** 送り仮名や英字の大小を整える作業は、読みやすさを上げない。

1	# Write a skill

3	A skill is a set of instructions this project has written for a particular kind of
4	work, loaded on demand rather than carried by every run. It lives under
5	`.github/atomaton/skills/<category>/<name>.md`, and `<category>/<name>` is the
6	name an agent asks for with `load_skill`.
7	
8	## When a skill rather than the role prompt
9	
10	The role prompt is what every run of an agent carries. A skill is what only some
11	runs need. So the test is whether the work in front of a run is of a kind the
12	instructions cover:
13	
14	- **A skill** — a procedure for a situation that arises sometimes: a dependency is
15	  missing, the answer is not in the repository, a pipeline has to be set up.
16	- **The role prompt** — what is true of every run of that agent: what it is for,
17	  what it must not do, which outcome ends a run.
18	
19	A check that is not optional does not belong behind an optional load. The
20	reviewer's mandatory checks are in its definition for exactly that reason: two
21	lines of one file asked for the same step by two mechanisms, and the one behind
22	the load was obeyed 43 times out of 227.
23

25	
26	```markdown
27	---
28	name: research/web-search
29	description: Load when the answer is not in your repository — fetching a page whose address you know, and running a general search when you do not.
30	---
31	
32	# Looking outside your repository
33	
34	...
35	```
36	
37	`name` is the name an agent asks for, and `description` is what the catalog shows
38	— it is the whole of what an agent sees before loading, so it has to say when to
39	load the skill, not what the skill contains. The body is the instructions, and it
40	arrives only when the agent asks.

43	
44	The template ships a few skills as a starting point, and `skills/project/` is
45	yours outright — an upgrade will not fight you for it. The shipped ones are
46	defaults the template also expects you to tune, so a change there is either an
47	improvement you have not taken or a change you made on purpose, and the two look
48	identical. [What an upgrade replaces, and what is
49	yours](../../runtime/boundaries.md) is the whole rule.

257	Your report is the only thing you leave that outlives the run, and it is what the

267	exists nowhere else — what you concluded, and how you know — in four parts, in
268	this order, every time. A part with nothing in it says so; none is dropped. Three
269	of the four have a ceiling, and a ceiling is a limit rather than a target.
270	
271	**What you concluded.** One or two sentences, first, saying what is true now and
272	what it means for whoever reads it. Not that you followed the steps and not that
273	the work is complete: how the run ended is already recorded above.
274	Two sentences is the ceiling, not the opening move of a longer one.
275	
276	**The conclusion is written for a person, not for a reader of the code.** What
277	happened and what it changes, in the words of the outcome; the machinery's names —
278	files, functions, flags — are anchors, and they belong in the evidence part beside
279	what backs them.
280	
281	**How you know.** Only the claims your conclusion rests on — not every claim the
282	message makes. Each of those anchored to something the reader can check without
283	asking you: a path with a line number, text copied out of a tool result, a number
284	with its unit, a command and what it exited with. Name the files. This is the
285	part folds exist for: when it runs longer than a reader wants open, fold it and
286	let the anchors live one click away — folded, not thinned.
287	
288	Write a path and a line as `path/to/file.ts:42`. GitHub turns that into a link to
289	the line, so the reader lands on it rather than opening the file and searching for
290	it — which is the difference between a claim they can check and one they will take
291	on trust. It is the one anchor the page can follow, so reach for it before prose
292	about where something is.
293	
294	A sentence saying only that you performed a step carries no checkable claim, and an
295	unanchored one costs the reader the work of establishing it again. Five items at most.
296	
297	**What you could not establish.** What you tried, what came back, and what is
298	still unknown because of it — a tool that refused you, a gate you could not read,
299	a search that kept returning unrelated files, a place where you assumed rather
300	than checked. Nobody else can recover this: you are the run that saw it, and the
301	result it arrived in is not kept. Write that there is nothing if there is
302	genuinely nothing; leaving the part out is itself a claim. This is the one part
303	with no ceiling, because it is the one that goes missing.

# Skill: project/conventions

# Repository conventions

This repository builds Atomaton, the delivery template. It is both the producer of
that template and an adopter of it, which creates rules that do not apply
anywhere else.

This file is not part of the template. Its source is `self/atomaton/skills/project/`,
and it is deliberately absent from `src/` so adopters never receive it.

## The four trees

| Tree | What it is | Who writes it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `src/**` | Source of the deliverable | You |
| `dist/.github/**` | The deliverable adopters receive | The build |
| `self/**` | This repository's own files, the ones that are not the template's | You |
| `.github/**` | This repository's running configuration | The self-deploy job, from a release plus `self/` |

Two different activities live in this table, and which one you are doing decides
which rules apply:

- **improving the deliverable** — `src/**`. It affects every adopter, and it
  reaches this repository only after a release and a self-deploy.
- **improving this repository's own operation** — `self/**`. It affects nobody
  else, and it applies as soon as it merges.

The rest of this file does not separate them cleanly. That is a known gap, tracked
in the documentation restructure; until then, read each rule and ask which of the two it is about.

`src/content/**` is mirrored verbatim into `dist/.github/atomaton/` and from there
into an adopter's repository. **It may only contain content that holds for any
project using Atomaton.** No reference to this repository's build pipeline, no
mention of `dist/`, `bun run synth`, or `build-dist.ts`, and no incident history
or PR numbers. If a rule is about developing *this* repository, it belongs in
this file instead.

## Generated output is not tracked

Change `src/**` only. `dist/**` is gitignored, so there is nothing generated to
commit and nothing to keep in sync.

Run `bun run synth` freely to inspect what adopters would receive. It writes only
into the ignored `dist/`, so it cannot dirty your commit.

Adopters receive the deliverable from a release, not from a merge, so nothing you
merge needs to carry it.

**Never touch `version` in `package.json`.** The version is the release declaration:
merging an edit to it publishes to adopters, and that decision belongs to a person,
made on the pull request the **Atomaton Release** workflow opens — never inside a
work pull request. A version left alone is a merge that publishes nothing, which is
the normal case. A work pull request that arrives with a version change in it is a
merge-blocking defect: flag it, and have the edit taken back out before merge.

`.github/**` is a different matter — see below. It is tracked, and every file in it
comes from either the release or `self/`.

## main is protected; everything lands by pull request

`.github/atomaton/rulesets/main.json` is the source of truth for what may reach main:
direct pushes are refused, and a pull request cannot merge until the `check` job
passes. It is applied by hand from an account with admin, and taken as correctly
configured thereafter — nothing verifies it, because a check could only report and
never enforce: with no ruleset, `check` would not be a required context either.

Changing the rule is a pull request against the JSON, followed by one `gh api`
call from an account with admin (see CONTRIBUTING.md). CI cannot make that call —
`administration` is not a permission a workflow can hold.

`check_merge_readiness` reports against whatever the ruleset currently
requires, so it follows the file rather than holding a second opinion.

Nothing bypasses it. No workflow writes to main — the release job attaches the deliverable
to a release instead — and your merge satisfies the rules like anyone else's. Do
not propose a bypass actor: it would mean naming a GitHub App ID or a deploy key,
values that exist only after manual setup, so the JSON would stop describing the
whole configuration.

The workflows that run agents are generated from `src/workflows/` and shipped.
`self/workflows/` holds the two that are not: `atomaton-self-deploy.yml` and
`probe-dumpable.yml`.

## Adding a static file to the deliverable

A new non-code file under `src/content/` must also be added to `build-dist.ts`'s
verbatim-copy list, or it never reaches `dist/` at all.
`tests/contract/deployment-contract.test.ts` enforces this.

## `atoma validate` is on the CLI

The `atoma` binary is on the agent's PATH — the runner installs it at
`/usr/local/bin/atoma` — and it has a `validate` subcommand that checks an agent
definition against a tools file without starting a run:

```bash
atoma validate --agent-def .github/atomaton/agent-definitions/engineer.md \
               --tools-file /tmp/tools.yaml
```

It resolves every name in the definition's `mcp_servers` against the tools file,
checks the template's placeholders, and reports what it finds. `atomaton-validate-pr`
runs it on every pull request that touches an agent definition, so a definition
that names a server `tools.yaml` does not define is a red check rather than a run
that aborts before a single tool starts.

There is no MCP tool for it, and that is deliberate: it is a check a person or a
workflow runs, not something an agent needs mid-run. Use it from the shell when
you are changing a definition and want the same answer CI will give.

## `.github/` is an adoption, not a mirror

Nothing regenerates `.github/` automatically. It is this repository's deliberate
adoption of the deliverable, so it lags `src/` until someone applies a release.

**That lag is the point.** A change to `src/` must not reconfigure the live agents
the moment it merges. Two breakages reached the running system exactly that way.

### Applying a release

Dispatch **Atomaton Self Deploy** (`self/workflows/atomaton-self-deploy.yml`) from the
Actions tab. It opens a pull request and merges nothing. `.github/**` is in
`merge.governed_paths`, so a person reviews it.

What it does:

```bash
rm -rf .github            # so a file the release DELETED is gone, not orphaned
unzip release.zip         # the deliverable
cp -r self/. .github/     # this repository's own, at the same paths
```

`.github/` is therefore exactly those two sources, with nothing kept alive by
remembering to. Before `self/` existed this was a `cp -r` followed by
`git checkout -- .github/atomaton/config.yaml`, and a file the template had removed
stayed in the tree with no diff to notice it by.

It needs `SELF_DEPLOY_TOKEN`, a PAT with the `workflow` scope, because
`GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot write `.github/workflows/**` — refused on identity, not by
path. No agent can reach that token: it is named in one file outside the
deliverable, and `atomaton-runner.yml` does not mention it.

### Changing something in `self/`

An overlay entry is a copy, not a build, so it needs no release. Change
`self/X` and `.github/X` **in the same pull request**, identically.

`tests/contract/self-overlay.test.ts` requires them byte-identical, in both
directions. Editing `.github/X` alone is worse than not editing it at all: the next
self-deploy overwrites it from `self/` and the change disappears without a diff.

A file added to `.github/` that is in no release and not in `self/` is not checked
for, because the next deploy removes it anyway and because `.github/**` is in
`merge.governed_paths` — no agent can merge a change there, so a person reads it first.

# yomiyasu（よみやす） [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-blue.svg)](./LICENSE) [![GitHub release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/nanaism/yomiyasu)](https://github.com/nanaism/yomiyasu/releases) [English](./README.en.md) ## これは何？ 『**yomiyasu（よみやす）**』はAIが生成した日本語の不自然な比喩、曖昧な主述関係、不要な装飾を直し、読みやすい文章に整えるスキルです。 主に技術記事、設計書・仕様書、PR説明文、社内レポートなどの実務的な文章を対象として設計されています。 Claude Code、Codex、CursorをはじめとするAIコーディング環境に読み込ませて使用してください。本体を入れられない環境のために、本体を短くした yomiyasu-mini と yomiyasu-pocket も公開しています（[本体を入れられない環境では](#本体を入れられない環境では)）。 開発の背景、AI生成文の読みにくさ、コーパスを使った検証については、次の解説記事で紹介しています。 - [AI-Slopな日本語を構造レベルで読みやすくするSkill『yomiyasu（よみやす）』を作りました（Zenn）](https://zenn.dev/algoartis/articles/0b1c731881b25c) *Built with curiosity at [ALGO ARTIS](https://www.algo-artis.com/)* [![ALGO ARTIS](./assets/algo-artis.png)](https://www.algo-artis.com/)
ALGO ARTISについて > 株式会社ALGO ARTISは、社会基盤の最適化に取り組むスタートアップです。 > > 電力・海運・化学プラントといった現場では、膨大な制約が絡み合う複雑な運用計画を、今なお熟練者が手作業で組み立てています。 > > そうした高度な現場業務を数理モデル化し、実用的なヒューリスティック最適化アルゴリズムと業務システムを一貫して開発しています。 > > 最適化技術を用いた社会インフラの変革に興味がある方は、[公式ウェブサイト](https://www.algo-artis.com/)や[採用情報](https://www.algo-artis.com/career/)をご覧ください。
## 背景と課題 文章を生成するAIは日常的な道具となりました。 一方で、AIで生成された文章には独特のクセが残りやすく、そのままでは実務や技術発信に使いにくい場面が多くあります。 これまでに様々な文体調整プロンプトやスキルが試されてきましたが、依然として「AI特有の読みにくさ」が残るケースが見られます。 従来のアプローチが抱えていた限界は、主に次の4点でした。 1. 禁止語の置き換えにとどまる対処 「手触り」「解像度」「泥臭い」といった表層の単語を禁止しても、別の曖昧な語へ置き換わるだけで、不自然な文構造そのものは解消されませんでした。 2. 編集ルールの過剰適用 修辞の規範を与えすぎると、モデルが指示を過剰に解釈し、かえって不自然な造語や大げさな文体を招いていました。 3. 主述関係の曖昧さと非生物主語 誰が何をどうするのかが省略されたまま、概念や道具が比喩的な動詞（壊れる、倒す、効くなど）と結びつき、読み手が文脈を大きく補って読む必要がありました。 4. 形式の偏重と情報密度の低下 太字や箇条書きが増える一方で、手順やコードの仕組みといった核心の部分は抽象的に書かれ、文章の量に比べて実際の情報が少なくなっていました。 ## 本スキルのアプローチ 元の意味を保ったまま、読み違えやすい箇所や、文の関係を追うのに負担がかかる箇所を直します。自然に読める部分は残します。 ### 7つの変換原則 1. 主述・修飾・条件の点検 主語と述語、修飾語と掛かる先、指示語と指す対象を対応づけます。条件・例外・否定・並列・数量・順序も、書き直す前後で同じように追えるか確かめます。主体や対象を補うのは、原文や提供文脈から確定できる範囲に限ります。 2. 文の働きと文体の保持 文ごとに説明・依頼・助言・予定を区別し、働きに合わない文末だけを直します。完了した変更作業、現在の動作や方針、今後の予定を時制と役割に合わせて書き分け、語尾を散らすこと自体を目的にしません。常体・敬体は変更の指定がなければ保ち、技術記事という分野だけを理由に敬体へ変えません。 3. 擬人化の整理 道具や概念に感情や意志を持たせた表現を直します。道具やシステムの客観的な動作を述べる非生物主語は残します。 4. 比喩を平易な言葉へ `壊れる`、`倒す`、`効く`、`溶かす`などを、元の含みや意味の広さを保って言い換えます。動詞を替えた後も、主体・対象・修飾先を変えず、語順を追いやすくできるか確かめます。 5. 前置き・否定対比の役割の確認 前置きを削るのは、削っても主張や比重が変わらない場合だけです。評価や必要な対比、比較から方針へ移る接続は残します。 6. 情報を勝手に足さない 主張・比重・言い切りの強さ・文の働きを保ち、原文にない主体・原因・条件・数値・感情などを足しません。ルールを「契約」、比較の基準を「正本」と大げさに呼ぶ場合は役割に合う語へ直し、文字どおりの意味や定義済みの専門用語は保ちます。意味を確定できない箇所は、原文にある未確定の状態や既知の動作を本文に残した暫定文とし、推敲の理由や確認事項は本文の後に添え、読者向けの本文には入れません。 7. 文長・読点・装飾の調整 平均文長30〜45文字、1文の読点0〜2個を目安にします。短い主語や主題のすぐあとに置いて間を作るだけの読点は外し、並んだ語句を区切る読点や、外すと掛かり先が変わる読点は残します。箇条書きの先頭のラベルとコロンは、値の項目や、物や作業の名前に説明が続く項目では残します。分類の語、出来事を名詞にまとめた語、短い述語のラベルは、外して説明と1文にまとめます。過剰な装飾記号を整理し、英単語や数値の前後の空白は元の書式や指定されたスタイルを保ちます。残す太字は表示される形に整えます。 バージョンごとの変更は [CHANGELOG.md](./CHANGELOG.md) にあります。 ## Before → After 例 2.0.0 のスキルで AI の文章を推敲した例です。Claude Code（Claude Opus 5.5）に「draft.md を yomiyasu で読みやすくして、結果を out.md に書いてください。」とだけ頼み、1回目の出力をそのまま載せています。 ### 例1: 業務・仕様解説 #### Before > ここで**重要なのは、単なるパーツの共通化ではなく、組織の意思決定OSとしてのガバナンス**です。 > > 従来の開発では、画面ごとに手触り感を探りながらパーツを作っていました。しかし、片方だけを見て画面を作ると、もう片方のアクセシビリティが**静かに壊れます**。そこでデザインシステムという**強固な土台**を置くことで、開発者の**解像度が一段上がります**。 > > デザインシステム導入のメリットは、主に次の3点です。 > - **開発速度の加速**: コンポーネントを再利用することで、時間を溶かさずに済みます。 > - **仕様の収斂**: 判断に迷うスタイルは、あらかじめ**共通側に倒します**。 > - **アクセシビリティの担保**: ガイドラインが規律を要求するため、事故を未然に防ぐことができます。 > > もちろん、これは「デザイナーが不要になる」ことを意味しません。日々の開発に**地味に効いてきます**。ぜひ参考にしてみてください！ #### After > ここでは、単なるパーツの共通化ではなく組織で意思決定をするときの枠組みとしてのガバナンスが重要です。 > > 従来の開発では、画面ごとに操作感を探りながらパーツを作っていました。しかし、片方だけを見て画面を作ると、もう片方のアクセシビリティが気づかないうちに損なわれます。そこでデザインシステムをしっかりした基本として用意すると、開発者の理解が一段深まります。 > > デザインシステム導入のメリットは主に次の3点です。 > - コンポーネントを再利用することで開発が速くなり、時間を無駄にせずに済みます。 > - 判断に迷うスタイルはあらかじめ共通のものに統一し、仕様をそろえます。 > - ガイドラインが規律を求めるため、アクセシビリティを保ち、事故を未然に防ぐことができます。 > > もちろん、これは「デザイナーが不要になる」ことを意味しません。日々の開発に目立たないながらも役立ってきます。ぜひ参考にしてみてください。 #### 変更説明 yomiyasu は比喩や造語（`意思決定OS`、`静かに壊れます`、`強固な土台`、`地味に効いてきます`）をふだんの言葉に直し、太字をすべて外しました。箇条書きは太字のラベルとコロンを外し、「開発が速くなり」のようにラベルの意味を説明の文に入れています。結びの「！」は「。」にしました。原文だけでは決められない`片方`と`もう片方`は書き換えず、何を指すかを書き手に確かめたい点として報告しています。 ### 例2: 技術解説 #### Before > 非同期処理における**最大の落とし穴**は、ネットワークの瞬断です。 > > **依存構造は分割できない。動かしながら引き返す。** > > 単にメッセージを流すだけでは、背後でデータが**静かに壊れます**。前提を、経路が代わりに添えてくれるわけではありません。 > > そこで**地味に効いてくる**のが、以下の3つの原則です。 > - **冪等性の担保**: 重複した処理は**黙ってスキップ**します。 > - **安全なリトライ**: 指数バックオフを挟むことで、DBの負荷を逃がします。 > - **DLQへの退避**: 破綻したメッセージは隔離し、原因を1つずつ**潰していきます**。 > > デバッグで丸一日**時間を溶かさない**ためにも、この境界線を意識した設計が不可欠です。いかがでしたでしょうか。 #### After > 非同期処理における最大の落とし穴は、ネットワークの瞬断です。 > > 依存構造は分割できない。動かしながら引き返す。 > > 単にメッセージを流すだけでは、気づかないうちにデータがおかしくなります。経路が前提を代わりに添えてくれるわけではありません。 > > そこで目立たないながらも役立つのが、以下の3つの原則です。 > - 冪等性の担保: 重複した処理は表に出さずにスキップします。 > - 安全なリトライ: 指数バックオフを挟むことで、DBの負荷を逃がします。 > - DLQへの退避: 破綻したメッセージは隔離し、原因を1つずつ取り除いていきます。 > > デバッグで丸一日を無駄にしないためにも、この境界線を意識した設計が不可欠です。 #### 変更説明 yomiyasu は太字を外し、比喩の動詞（`静かに壊れます`、`地味に効いてくる`、`黙ってスキップ`、`潰していきます`、`時間を溶かさない`）を言い換えました。最後の`いかがでしたでしょうか`は中身のない決まり文句として消しています。箇条書きは原則の名前に説明が続く形なので、ラベルとコロンを残しました。2行目の`依存構造は分割できない。動かしながら引き返す。`は何を言っているかが読み取れないので書き換えず、最後の文の`この境界線`が何を指すかとあわせて、書き手に尋ねています。 skills add`（推奨） ```bash # 新規インストール npx skills add nanaism/yomiyasu # 最新版へのアップデート npx skills update yomiyasu ``` Claude Codeなどのエージェントの設定ディレクトリへ、スキルをインストール・更新します。スキル定義は `skills/yomiyasu/SKILL.md`
